sentences.text: Protoceratops were small ceratopsians reaching lengths of 2 to 2.5 meters and weighing between 62 and 104 kilograms. They are characterized by a proportionally large skull, a short stiff neck, and a neck frill.
Protoceratops possessed a horn-like structure over the nose that was single in P. andrewsi but double and paired in P. hellenikorhinus.
These herbivores had prominent jaws and teeth adapted for chopping foliage and plant material.
The genus Protoceratops was named by Granger and Gregory in 1923.
On September 2, photographer James B. Shackelford discovered the holotype skull (AMNH 6251) of Protoceratops in reddish sandstones.
Significant remains were later found in the Tugriken Shireh locality of the Djadokhta Formation and in the Khulsan locality of the Barun Goyot Formation in Mongolia.
In 1975, Polish paleontologists Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska described the species Protoceratops kozlowskii.
Protoceratops lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 to 71 million years ago.
Adult Protoceratops were primarily quadrupedal, though juveniles could walk bipedally if needed.
The neck frill was likely used for display, intraspecific combat, neck protection, and anchoring jaw muscles.
Protoceratops were once thought to be nocturnal due to their large scleral rings, but are now believed to be cathemeral, active at dawn and dusk.
Protoceratops appear to have cared for their young and laid soft-shelled eggs, a rare trait among dinosaurs.

Granger and Gregory agreed with Osborn that further exploration of Asia could resolve major evolutionary gaps in the fossil record. Because Protoceratops was considered more primitive than other known ceratopsians, they established the family Protoceratopsidae, characterized by the lack of horns.
It was initially believed that Protoceratops was an ancestor of ankylosaurians and larger ceratopsians like Triceratops, but this view changed after the discovery of other protoceratopsids.
In 2006, Peter Makovicky and Mark A. Norell suggested that Bainoceratops might be a synonym of Protoceratops.
In 1994, Norell and colleagues found an oviraptorid embryo in an egg, proving that the eggs previously thought to belong to Protoceratops actually belonged to Oviraptor.
In 2008, Darla K. Zelenitsky and François Therrien concluded that the egg genus Protoceratopsidovum belonged to a maniraptoran dinosaur more derived than oviraptorids, not Protoceratops.
